text:
Three years ago, I joined a small fintech startup with a lot to learn and plenty of room to grow. Today, I’m excited to share that I’ve been promoted to Senior Software Engineer.

I’m grateful to the teammates who challenged me, trusted me with meaningful work, and made the hard problems fun to solve. Looking forward to what we build next.

After a rewarding chapter at Deloitte, I’m taking the leap and starting my own consulting firm.

I’ve learned a lot from the people I’ve worked with and the clients who trusted me with their toughest problems. Now I’m excited to bring that experience to a new kind of work, on my own terms.

More soon. For now, I’m grateful, a little nervous, and very ready to get started.

I was laid off last month. It wasn’t part of my plan, and I’d be lying if I said the first few days were easy.

A few things have become clearer since then: my job mattered, but it wasn’t my whole identity. Asking for help is easier than I expected. And a thoughtful note from someone can mean a lot when the ground shifts under you.

I’m taking a breath, reconnecting with people, and figuring out what’s next. If you’ve been through this too, I’d be glad to hear what helped.

Most companies don’t have a remote-work problem. They have an office habit problem.

They move meetings online, keep the same meeting load, and call it flexibility. They measure presence through green dots instead of making expectations clear. Then they wonder why people feel disconnected.

Remote work gets better when teams write things down, make decisions visible, and leave room for focused work. The tools matter less than the habits around them.

We’re hiring two backend engineers in Berlin!

You’ll work with Go and Postgres on systems that support a growing product, alongside a team that cares about thoughtful engineering and shipping useful things.

If you’re curious, or know someone who might be a fit, send me a message and I’ll share more about the roles.

My first manager taught me that leadership often looks like making the work easier for someone else.

When I was new, she didn’t swoop in with answers. She asked good questions, gave me room to try, and stepped in when I was stuck for real. I still remember how much that trust changed the way I approached a hard problem.

I try to pass that on now: be clear, be available, and let people own the work.

We’re excited to share that we’ve raised a $4M seed round led by Accel.

This gives us the runway to build faster, grow the team, and keep working on a problem we believe matters. Huge thanks to our investors, early customers, and everyone who helped us get here.

There’s a lot ahead. Back to work.

AI is changing marketing, but the most useful shift may be less glamorous than the demos suggest.

It can help teams draft, test variations, summarize research, and move faster through repetitive tasks. That’s valuable. But speed doesn’t tell you what your audience cares about, whether a claim is true, or which idea is worth pursuing.

The teams I’m watching closely are using AI to make more room for judgment: better questions, sharper strategy, and closer attention to customers. The tool can help produce the work. People still have to decide what deserves to be made.

We shipped our new mobile app today!

Proud of this team for all the thoughtful work, late fixes, and small details that went into getting it across the line. Can’t wait to see what people do with it.

A few things I wish I’d heard as a junior developer:

1. Ask questions early. It saves everyone time.
2. Read the code around the code you’re changing.
3. Make small, reviewable pull requests.
4. Learn to explain your decisions, not just your solution.
5. Keep a list of what you’ve learned. You’ll be surprised how far you’ve come.

You don’t need to know everything. You do need to stay curious.

My first startup is closing after two years.

I’m proud of what we built, and sad that we couldn’t make the business work. We got some things right and made plenty of mistakes: we moved too slowly on a few hard decisions, and we didn’t listen closely enough when the evidence changed.

The people mattered most. I’m grateful to my cofounder, our small team, our customers, and everyone who gave us a chance. I’m still processing it, but I know I’ll carry what I learned into whatever comes next.

Mental health at work isn’t a side topic. It affects how people feel, how they work, and whether they can keep doing their jobs sustainably.

Managers don’t need to have all the answers. They can start by making workloads realistic, listening without judgment, and treating time off as normal. A supportive culture is built in everyday choices, not just a line in a benefits page.

A customer service interaction recently reminded me what good business looks like.

I had a small issue with an order. The person who helped me listened, took ownership, and fixed it without making me repeat the story three times. It took a few minutes, but it changed how I felt about the company.

Customers remember how you handle the moment when something goes wrong. The best service doesn’t just solve the problem; it makes trust feel well placed.

I’ve finished my MBA at INSEAD, and I’m feeling grateful for the people who made this chapter what it was.

To my classmates: thank you for the conversations, the different perspectives, and the laughs between deadlines. To the faculty and staff, thank you for pushing us to think more carefully. And to my family and friends, thank you for your patience and encouragement from afar.

I’m leaving with new questions, a wider circle of people I admire, and a lot to think about.

A contrarian take on hustle culture: sometimes the most ambitious thing you can do is stop working for the day.

Being constantly busy can feel like progress, but it often leaves little room to think, recover, or notice that you’re solving the wrong problem. Rest isn’t a reward for finishing everything. There will always be more.

I’d rather build a pace I can sustain than celebrate being exhausted.

My newsletter just reached 10,000 subscribers. I’m excited, and a little amazed that so many people have made room for it in their inbox.

It grew one issue at a time: writing consistently, paying attention to what readers replied to, and improving the parts that weren’t working. There wasn’t a magic growth trick. Just a lot of drafts and helpful feedback.

Thank you for reading and sharing it. I’m looking forward to the next issue.

Networking as an introvert works better for me when I keep it simple.

I try to have one good conversation instead of working the whole room. I reach out with a specific reason for connecting. I ask questions I’m genuinely curious about. And I follow up when I said I would.

You don’t have to become the loudest person at an event to build meaningful relationships. Being thoughtful and consistent counts.

Working in sales taught me that listening is more useful than having the perfect pitch.

People will tell you what matters if you give them space to explain it. Sometimes what they need isn’t what you expected. Sometimes the right answer is that your product isn’t a fit.

That lesson travels well beyond sales: understand the problem before rushing to offer a solution.

Our nonprofit has reached 1,000 volunteers!

That number represents a thousand people who chose to give their time, skills, and care to this work. I’m grateful to everyone who showed up, welcomed someone new, or helped keep things moving behind the scenes.

This milestone belongs to all of you. There’s more to do, and I’m glad we’re doing it together.

I’m back at work after parental leave, and it feels good to be finding my rhythm again.

The time away changed how I think about attention, energy, and what deserves to be urgent. I’m grateful to my colleagues for making the transition feel welcoming, and to my family for carrying me through the new routines.

I’m easing back in and taking it one week at a time.

Small agency folks: what CRM are you using, and would you recommend it?

We’re looking for something straightforward that helps us track leads, manage follow-ups, and keep client conversations organized without a lot of setup.

Would love to hear what’s worked for your team, especially if you’ve switched from another tool.

Product managers should learn enough SQL to answer basic questions for themselves.

You don’t need to replace your data team. But being able to check a hypothesis, explore a trend, or spot a surprising result can make discussions more concrete and help you ask better questions.

The point isn’t to produce a dashboard for everything. It’s to get closer to the evidence behind the decisions you’re making.

Deep Work by Cal Newport changed how I think about a productive day.

I used to judge it by how many things I got through. The book made me pay more attention to whether I’d made time for the work that needed real concentration. That shift hasn’t made my calendar magically quiet, but it has made me more deliberate about protecting a few uninterrupted blocks.

A useful reminder that being occupied and making progress aren’t always the same thing.

Ten years as a nurse.

I’ve cared for people on ordinary days and some of the hardest days of their lives. I’ve learned that skill matters, and so does showing up with patience when someone is scared or tired. I’ve also learned how much nurses rely on one another.

I’m grateful to my colleagues, patients, and families who have taught me along the way. A decade in, I still feel lucky to do this work.

As a recruiter, one of the biggest interview mistakes I see is trying to give the answer you think we want instead of answering the question honestly.

It’s fine not to know something. Talk through how you’d approach it. Be clear about what you did and what the team did. If a project didn’t go as planned, explain what you learned.

A thoughtful, specific answer tells me much more than a polished one that avoids the question.

We’re hosting a free webinar next Thursday on cloud cost optimization.

We’ll walk through practical ways to understand where cloud spend is going, find common sources of waste, and make changes without slowing teams down. There’ll be time for questions, too.

If that sounds useful, send me a message and I’ll share the registration link. Hope to see you there!

I’ve made the move from teaching to UX design.

The transition took time, plenty of learning after work, and more than a few moments of wondering whether I was ready. Teaching gave me a foundation I use every day: listening closely, making complicated things easier to understand, and paying attention to how people actually experience something.

I’m excited to bring that perspective into my new role and keep learning from the people around me.

Learning to say no has made me better at saying yes to the things I care about.

I used to treat every request as something I should fit in somehow. Eventually, my attention got spread too thin to do any of it well. Now I try to be clear about my capacity and make choices with the bigger priorities in mind.

A respectful no can be more useful than an unreliable yes.

Huge congratulations to my former colleague Priya on her new role as CTO!

I had the pleasure of working with Priya and saw firsthand how thoughtful, steady, and sharp she is. Any team would be lucky to have her leading the way.

Wishing you all the best in the new role, Priya!

One year into freelancing as a designer, here are a few things I’ve learned: the work is only part of the job, a clear scope saves everyone stress, and following up on an invoice is a normal business task.

I’ve also learned to ask for feedback earlier and to leave some breathing room between projects. It’s been a year of figuring things out as I go, with help from clients and other freelancers who were generous with advice.

Still learning, and glad I made the jump.
